overview.text: The human heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the space known as the mediastinum.
overview.label: 19.1 Location of the Heart

overview.text: The dorsal surface of the heart lies near the bodies of the vertebrae, and its anterior surface sits deep to the sternum and costal cartilages.
overview.label: 19.1 Location of the Heart

overview.text: The great veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the great arteries, the aorta and pulmonary trunk, are attached to the superior surface of the heart, called the base.
overview.label: 19.1 Location of the Heart

overview.text: The inferior tip of the heart, the apex, lies just to the left of the sternum between the junction of the fourth and fifth ribs near their articulation with the costal cartilages.
overview.label: 19.1 Location of the Heart

overview.text: A typical heart is approximately the size of your fist: 12 cm (5 in) in length, 8 cm (3.5 in) wide, and 6 cm (2.5 in) in thickness.
overview.label: 19.1 Shape and Size of the Heart

overview.text: The human heart consists of four chambers: The left side and the right side each have one atrium and one ventricle.
overview.label: 19.1 Chambers and Circulation through the Heart

overview.text: The ventricles serve as the primary pumping chambers of the heart, propelling blood to the lungs or to the rest of the body.
overview.label: 19.1 Chambers and Circulation through the Heart

ra.text: The right atrium serves as the receiving chamber for blood returning to the heart from the systemic circulation.
ra.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

ra.text: The two major systemic veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the large coronary vein called the coronary sinus that drains the heart myocardium empty into the right atrium.
ra.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

ra.text: The opening between the atrium and ventricle is guarded by the tricuspid valve.
ra.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

rv.text: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve.
rv.label: 19.1 Right Ventricle

rv.text: When the right ventricle contracts, it ejects blood into the pulmonary trunk, which branches into the left and right pulmonary arteries that carry it to each lung.
rv.label: 19.1 Right Ventricle

la.text: After exchange of gases in the pulmonary capillaries, blood returns to the left atrium high in oxygen via one of the four pulmonary veins.
la.label: 19.1 Left Atrium

la.text: The opening between the left atrium and ventricle is guarded by the mitral valve.
la.label: 19.1 Left Atrium

lv.text: The left ventricle is the major pumping chamber for the systemic circuit; it ejects blood into the aorta through the aortic semilunar valve.
lv.label: 19.1 Left Ventricle

lv.text: Although the ventricles on the right and left sides pump the same amount of blood per contraction, the muscle of the left ventricle is much thicker and better developed than that of the right ventricle.
lv.label: 19.1 Layers

vwall.text: Although the ventricles on the right and left sides pump the same amount of blood per contraction, the muscle of the left ventricle is much thicker and better developed than that of the right ventricle.
vwall.label: 19.1 Layers

vwall.text: The middle and thickest layer is the myocardium, made largely of cardiac muscle cells.
vwall.label: 19.1 Layers

vwall.text: It is the contraction of the myocardium that pumps blood through the heart and into the major arteries.
vwall.label: 19.1 Layers

vwall.text: Between the two ventricles is a second septum known as the interventricular septum.
vwall.label: 19.1 Septa of the Heart

vwall.text: It is substantially thicker than the interatrial septum, since the ventricles generate far greater pressure when they contract.
vwall.label: 19.1 Septa of the Heart

tricuspid.text: Between the right atrium and the right ventricle is the right atrioventricular valve, or tricuspid valve.
tricuspid.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

tricuspid.text: It typically consists of three flaps, or leaflets, made of endocardium reinforced with additional connective tissue.
tricuspid.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

tricuspid.text: The flaps are connected by chordae tendineae to the papillary muscles, which control the opening and closing of the valves.
tricuspid.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

mitral.text: Located at the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle is the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve or the left atrioventricular valve.
mitral.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

mitral.text: Structurally, this valve consists of two cusps, compared to the three cusps of the tricuspid valve.
mitral.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

mitral.text: The two cusps of the mitral valve are attached by chordae tendineae to two papillary muscles that project from the wall of the ventricle.
mitral.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

pvalve.text: Emerging from the right ventricle at the base of the pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve, or the pulmonary valve; it is also known as the pulmonic valve or the right semilunar valve.
pvalve.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

pvalve.text: The pulmonary valve is comprised of three small flaps of endothelium reinforced with connective tissue.
pvalve.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

pvalve.text: Unlike the atrioventricular valves, there are no papillary muscles or chordae tendineae associated with the pulmonary valve.
pvalve.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

avalve.text: At the base of the aorta is the aortic semilunar valve, or the aortic valve, which prevents backflow from the aorta.
avalve.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

avalve.text: It normally is composed of three flaps.
avalve.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

avalve.text: When the ventricle relaxes and blood attempts to flow back into the ventricle from the aorta, blood will fill the cusps of the valve, causing it to close and producing an audible sound.
avalve.label: 19.1 Heart Valve Structure and Function

pap-rv.text: Each flap of the valve is attached to strong strands of connective tissue, the chordae tendineae, literally “tendinous cords,” or sometimes more poetically referred to as “heart strings.”
pap-rv.label: 19.1 Right Ventricle

pap-rv.text: They connect each of the flaps to a papillary muscle that extends from the inferior ventricular surface.
pap-rv.label: 19.1 Right Ventricle

pap-rv.text: There are three papillary muscles in the right ventricle, called the anterior, posterior, and septal muscles, which correspond to the three sections of the valves.
pap-rv.label: 19.1 Right Ventricle

pap-lv.text: The mitral valve is connected to papillary muscles via chordae tendineae.
pap-lv.label: 19.1 Left Ventricle

pap-lv.text: There are two papillary muscles on the left—the anterior and posterior—as opposed to three on the right.
pap-lv.label: 19.1 Left Ventricle

coronary.text: Coronary arteries supply blood to the myocardium and other components of the heart.
coronary.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

coronary.text: The first portion of the aorta after it arises from the left ventricle gives rise to the coronary arteries.
coronary.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

coronary.text: Coronary vessel branches that remain on the surface of the artery and follow the sulci are called epicardial coronary arteries.
coronary.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

lca.text: The left coronary artery distributes blood to the left side of the heart, the left atrium and ventricle, and the interventricular septum.
lca.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

circumflex.text: The circumflex artery arises from the left coronary artery and follows the coronary sulcus to the left.
circumflex.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

circumflex.text: Eventually, it will fuse with the small branches of the right coronary artery.
circumflex.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

lad.text: The larger anterior interventricular artery, also known as the left anterior descending artery (LAD), is the second major branch arising from the left coronary artery.
lad.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

lad.text: It follows the anterior interventricular sulcus around the pulmonary trunk.
lad.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

lad.text: Along the way it gives rise to numerous smaller branches that interconnect with the branches of the posterior interventricular artery, forming anastomoses.
lad.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

rca.text: The right coronary artery proceeds along the coronary sulcus and distributes blood to the right atrium, portions of both ventricles, and the heart conduction system.
rca.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

marginal.text: Normally, one or more marginal arteries arise from the right coronary artery inferior to the right atrium.
marginal.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

marginal.text: The marginal arteries supply blood to the superficial portions of the right ventricle.
marginal.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

pda.text: On the posterior surface of the heart, the right coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery, also known as the posterior descending artery.
pda.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

pda.text: It runs along the posterior portion of the interventricular sulcus toward the apex of the heart, giving rise to branches that supply the interventricular septum and portions of both ventricles.
pda.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries

cveins.text: Cardiac veins parallel the small cardiac arteries and generally drain into the coronary sinus.
cveins.label: 19.1 Chapter Review

gcv.text: The great cardiac vein can be seen initially on the surface of the heart following the interventricular sulcus, but it eventually flows along the coronary sulcus into the coronary sinus on the posterior surface.
gcv.label: 19.1 Coronary Veins

gcv.text: The great cardiac vein initially parallels the anterior interventricular artery and drains the areas supplied by this vessel.
gcv.label: 19.1 Coronary Veins

scv.text: The small cardiac vein parallels the right coronary artery and drains the blood from the posterior surfaces of the right atrium and ventricle.
scv.label: 19.1 Coronary Veins

sinus.text: The coronary sinus is a large, thin-walled vein on the posterior surface of the heart lying within the atrioventricular sulcus and emptying directly into the right atrium.
sinus.label: 19.1 Coronary Veins

sinus.text: Immediately superior and slightly medial to the opening of the inferior vena cava on the posterior surface of the atrium is the opening of the coronary sinus.
sinus.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

svc.text: The superior vena cava drains blood from regions superior to the diaphragm: the head, neck, upper limbs, and the thoracic region.
svc.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

svc.text: It empties into the superior and posterior portions of the right atrium.
svc.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

ivc.text: The inferior vena cava drains blood from areas inferior to the diaphragm: the lower limbs and abdominopelvic region of the body.
ivc.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

ivc.text: It, too, empties into the posterior portion of the atria, but inferior to the opening of the superior vena cava.
ivc.label: 19.1 Right Atrium

ptrunk.text: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk, which leads toward the lungs and bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries.
ptrunk.label: 19.1 Chambers and Circulation through the Heart

ptrunk.text: The pulmonary trunk arteries and their branches are the only arteries in the post-natal body that carry relatively deoxygenated blood.
ptrunk.label: 19.1 Chambers and Circulation through the Heart

pveins.text: Highly oxygenated blood returning from the pulmonary capillaries in the lungs passes through a series of vessels that join together to form the pulmonary veins—the only post-natal veins in the body that carry highly oxygenated blood.
pveins.label: 19.1 Chambers and Circulation through the Heart

pveins.text: After exchange of gases in the pulmonary capillaries, blood returns to the left atrium high in oxygen via one of the four pulmonary veins.
pveins.label: 19.1 Left Atrium

aorta.text: The left ventricle is the major pumping chamber for the systemic circuit; it ejects blood into the aorta through the aortic semilunar valve.
aorta.label: 19.1 Left Ventricle

aorta.text: The first portion of the aorta after it arises from the left ventricle gives rise to the coronary arteries.
aorta.label: 19.1 Coronary Arteries
